title: The reading room and the reading public
bodyMd:
Before the eighteenth century a book was, for most of the people who encountered one, an object heard rather than read. A single copy served a household, a workshop or a parish; someone read aloud and the rest listened, interrupted and argued. Reading was an occasion, and like most occasions it had a governing voice.

The subscription reading rooms that spread through provincial towns after about 1740 changed the arithmetic of this arrangement without, at first, changing its manners. A room held perhaps forty periodicals and a few hundred volumes, paid for by an annual subscription that put it within reach of shopkeepers and clerks as well as of the gentry. What the rooms made possible was not cheaper reading — the same money spent directly on books would have bought more pages — but simultaneous reading. Forty men could hold forty different opinions about the same week's news because forty different periodicals had reached them on the same morning.

Historians have often treated these rooms as nurseries of political argument, and the surviving minute books lend the claim some support: disputes over whether a particular journal should be taken were recorded with a solemnity suggesting that more was at stake than shelf space. But the more consequential change may have been the quieter one. A subscriber who disliked what he read could not answer the author; he could only turn the page and read someone else. The habit of comparison — of holding one account of an event beside another and noticing the distance between them — is a habit the rooms taught almost accidentally, simply by putting rival accounts within arm's reach.

That habit outlived the institution. By 1850 most of the rooms had closed, undercut by cheap newspapers and by public libraries that lent books instead of lending chairs. What had been learned in them, however, was not how to read a particular periodical but how to distrust one.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph history passage of about 320 words on eighteenth-century subscription reading rooms. The first paragraph describes reading before 1700 as a shared, spoken occasion with one governing voice. The second paragraph explains that subscription reading rooms, spreading after about 1740, held roughly forty periodicals and a few hundred volumes and were affordable to shopkeepers and clerks as well as the gentry; their contribution was not cheaper reading but simultaneous reading, since forty readers could read forty different periodicals on the same morning. The third paragraph reports that historians treat the rooms as nurseries of political argument, supported by minute books recording solemn disputes about which journals to take, but argues the more consequential change was quieter: because a reader could not answer an author, only turn to a rival account, the rooms accidentally taught the habit of comparison. The fourth paragraph notes that most rooms had closed by 1850, displaced by cheap newspapers and by lending libraries, and concludes that what was learned there was not how to read a particular periodical but how to distrust one.
